consensus_summary: All four blind responses identify the ship primarily as the Church — the vessel of salvation carrying believers safely through the sea of the world toward eternal life, rooted in Noah's-ark typology (1 Pet 3:20-21), the Gospel storm narratives, and the 'Barque of Peter' tradition. Secondary meanings listed include the individual life/soul's voyage, worldly commerce and pride (ships of Tarshish, Tyre in Ezek 27, Babylon in Rev 18), and refuge/salvation more generally.
book_summary: The book defines the ship as an organized kingdom, city, or state riding upon the sea of peoples — its rulers steer it, its inhabitants crew it. Christ needs no vessel to rule the waters, but when He boards one it comes under its true Head. The book explicitly flags 'the Church, a vessel carrying believers safely through the world' as the commonly taught view it departs from, and cites Ezek 27 (Tyre as ship), Isa 23, Acts 27, Rev 18, and Jonah 1.
consensus_core_identification: Ship = the Church, the vessel of salvation preserving believers through the world/sea.
book_core_identification: Ship = an organized political entity (kingdom, city, or state) sailing upon the sea of peoples, headed by whoever steers it — rightly headed only when Christ boards.
boundary_disagreement: The book generalizes the political reading: not merely 'commerce/pride destined for judgment' (a consensus alternative) but any organized polity as such. It reclassifies the Gospel-boat and Acts 27 material — cases the consensus treats as ecclesial or providential — as instances of Christ boarding a human polity, and it drops the Church as the referent entirely.
material_contradiction: The consensus asserts the ship symbolizes the Church as the vessel of salvation; the book asserts the ship symbolizes a kingdom/city/state and explicitly rejects the Church reading in its common-view note. Both cannot identify the same symbol in the same sense: an organized worldly polity riding on the sea of peoples is not the Church, and the book's framing (Christ can rule the waters without any vessel) undercuts the idea that the ship is itself the means of salvation.
rationale: The core identifications are replacements, not refinements. The consensus's central referent (the Church) is explicitly named and set aside by the book, which substitutes a political-entity referent. The book's reading overlaps with the consensus's secondary Tyre/Babylon-commerce alternative in the cases it draws on (Ezek 27, Isa 23, Rev 18), but that alternative treats ships as emblems of commerce and pride, not as a general symbol of organized polities, and it never displaces the ecclesial primary. Because accepting the book requires rejecting the consensus's primary identification while partially reabsorbing some consensus-covered cases under a new category, this is DIVERGENT with PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION rather than REFINED or NOVEL.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED or even coverage by a listed alternative: Ezekiel 27 (Tyre depicted as a ship) and Rev 18 are cited by every consensus response as an established secondary meaning, so the book might be seen as merely elevating a recognized alternative to primary status and generalizing it slightly, rather than contradicting the tradition outright.
